intent: Test whether seven sensors spanning ±0.03 m at y=0.07 m, a larger wheel radius (0.035 m) for higher ground speed, and a slightly wider track (0.11 m) for turn stability let the robot keep the line on the s-bend and oval. Changes from iteration 1: sensors moved from 5 to 7 with y 0.06 to 0.07 m and 0.01 m spacing; wheel_radius 0.03 to 0.035 m; wheel_track 0.10 to 0.11 m. Body width, body length and mass are unchanged.
learning: Next iteration, check: (a) whether max_error still reaches 0.06 m on the s-bend, which would mean turn authority is still limiting; (b) whether progress rises on the oval and slalom, which would confirm that the extra lookahead helps; (c) whether the larger wheel radius gives enough speed to approach completion, measured by completion_time; (d) whether steering_oscillation rises with the wider track, which would mean the turn response is now too slow. Ask the Integrator whether the seven-sensor signal saturates at the outer sensors, and whether the 0.01 m spacing gives a smoother signal than the 0.015 m spacing used before.
rationale:
The evidence is consistent across both geometries. All 120 development trials (60 per design, across iterations 0 and 1) ended off_track with progress between 0.04 and 0.15. Max error sits at about 0.06 m, which is the off-track floor, and rms_error is about 0.02 to 0.03 m. Steering oscillation is low (0.07 to 0.16), so the robot is not jittering. It is drifting steadily outward, and the s-bend fails earliest. Iteration 1 improved on iteration 0 (score 55.8 vs 35.8), and its changes (sensors further ahead at y=0.06, wider span of ±0.03 m, a lighter and shorter body, and a narrower track) moved in the right direction. The remaining gap is mainly lookahead and speed, not sensing failure. Line loss is rare (about 1 event per run), so the sensors are still seeing the tape.

Changes in this proposal, each tied to that evidence:
1. Lookahead: move the sensors from y=0.06 to y=0.07 m. Seeing the line earlier gives the controller more time to react before the robot reaches a bend, and the s-bend failure is the clearest sign that reaction time is short.
2. Sensor count: move to 7 sensors at x = -0.03, -0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03 m. A 0.01 m spacing with a 0.012 m footprint gives overlapping coverage, so the signal stays usable as the robot drifts sideways. The extra sensors add noise averaging without adding much cost. Weights will be set by the Integrator.
3. Speed: raise wheel_radius from 0.03 to 0.035 m. Ground speed equals wheel radius times rotation rate, so a larger wheel gives more forward speed at the same PWM. The average speed needed to finish in 3 s is about 1.5 m/s, and every run so far has stalled far short of that. This is the main lever for completion_time, which the score rewards only if the run finishes.
4. Stability: widen wheel_track from 0.10 to 0.11 m. Turn rate is the wheel speed difference divided by track, so a wider track makes each unit of wheel differential turn the robot more slowly. That gives back some stability on the sharp s-bend, offsetting the faster response from the lighter body. Mass stays at 0.6 kg and body_length at 0.14 m to keep yaw inertia low.
5. Body width stays at 0.12 m. The off-track limit is max(0.06, tape_half_width + body_width/4), which is 0.06 m at this width, so widening the body gives no benefit.

Expected result: fewer off_track endings and more progress on s-bend and slalom, with the first completions possible on the oval. Completion is the main risk, because the larger wheel and longer lookahead must be matched by controller speed. I expect the Integrator to need a lower base_speed on the s-bend.
